analysis.one_liner: Cuts large farm subsidies, raises SNAP food benefits, and funds conservation, beginning farmers, and animal welfare.
analysis.headline: The bill went nowhere: referred to four House committees in March 2023, it never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with 5 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill is Representative Blumenauer's alternative farm bill. It would repeal two major commodity subsidy programs, cap total farm subsidy payments at $125,000 per recipient per year, and lower the income limit for subsidy eligibility, while extending crop insurance premium subsidies to farmers who plant erosion-reducing crops. On the nutrition side it would increase SNAP food benefits, fund healthy food access and school meals, and create tax credits to help beginning, veteran, and socially disadvantaged farmers buy farmland. It would also boost conservation funding and enforcement, create a USDA Office of Food Waste, require animal welfare standards at federal research centers, and expand local and regional food systems.
analysis.who_benefits: SNP recipients and food-insecure households, beginning and small farmers who struggle to buy land, socially disadvantaged and veteran farmers, organic farmers, and communities whose drinking water is affected by farm runoff.
analysis.who_benefits_short: SNAP households and small, beginning farmers

how_it_helps.text: The bill would increase SNAP benefits under a section titled 'Closing the meal gap,' and expand programs that let SNAP dollars buy more produce at farmers markets and retail stores.

It would create tax credits for selling and buying qualified farming property, aimed at beginning farmers and ranchers, veteran farmers, and socially disadvantaged farmers, to make it easier for new farmers to get land.

It would set multi-year funding for conservation programs (for example $3.2 billion per year for EQIP), require subsidy recipients to comply with conservation plans, and bar large feeding operations from getting payments to build animal waste facilities.
It would require USDA to follow animal welfare standards at federal agricultural research centers and create a tax credit for independent humane certification programs.
It would require annual public reporting of greenhouse gas emissions from livestock operations, fertilizer, and tillage, giving the public data on agricultural emissions.

analysis.who_pays: Large commodity farms and wealthy subsidy recipients, who would lose payments from the repealed subsidy programs and face the new $125,000 cap and $400,000 income limit; crop insurers and large livestock operations, which would face new restrictions and reporting; and taxpayers, who would fund expanded nutrition and conservation programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large commodity farms and crop insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the Agriculture Risk Coverage and Price Loss Coverage programs, keeping them only through the 2023 crop year, without creating a replacement price safety net; commodity farmers would be left with crop insurance alone during a price collapse or multi-year downturn.

The $125,000 total payment cap and $400,000 income limit apply to all subsidy recipients, which farm groups could reasonably argue reaches legitimate mid-size family farms, not only the largest operations.

New conservation compliance rules, including 50-foot vegetative buffers along waterways and fixed deadlines for compliance, add requirements and paperwork for working farmers who currently face lighter rules.

The bill authorizes new mandatory spending for nutrition, conservation, school meals, and loan programs using Commodity Credit Corporation funds, adding to federal farm-program spending even as it cuts subsidies elsewhere.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades subsidies that flow mainly to large commodity operations for broader nutrition, conservation, and beginning-farmer support, and it tries to pay for part of that shift by closing subsidy loopholes. Its real design weakness is the missing replacement safety net for commodity farmers: eliminating ARC and PLC without a successor program leaves agriculture exposed to a price crash, which supporters would answer with crop insurance but which critics would call an underpriced bet. The benefit-to-cost balance favors ordinary people, but the transition risk to mid-size farms is a genuine cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees in March 2023; none of them ever took it up, the only later action was a referral to a subcommittee in the final weeks of 2024, and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Earl Blumenauer introduced the Food and Farm Act in the House on March 28, 2023.
The bill was referred to the Agriculture Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, and Foreign Affairs Committees.
Five House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

No committee reported the bill, no hearing or markup appears in the action history, and the only subsequent action was a December 17, 2024 referral to the Subcommittee on Work and Welfare, weeks before the Congress ended.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large commodity operations and wealthy subsidy recipients kept the existing farm subsidy structure untouched, since the bill that would have capped and cut their payments never advanced. The crop insurance industry also kept the status quo, including the loopholes the bill would have closed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large farm-subsidy recipients and crop insurers

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup and never reported the bill during the full 21 months it had jurisdiction, before the final-week subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Democrat, and no Republican cosponsor or committee action appears in the record; the bill died in committees led by the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill repeals the ARC and PLC subsidy programs, caps total farm payments at $125,000 per recipient per year, and lowers the income eligibility cap from $900,000 to $400,000, directly cutting the federal checks going to the largest recipients. These operations have historically received the bulk of commodity subsidies, so the reform's savings come mainly from them.

The bill closes insurer-friendly loopholes, including yield transfers between parcels, subsidies on unsuitable land, and generous prevented-planting payments, but it also expands the whole-farm insurance option with no liability limit and extends premium subsidies to cover-crop planting, routing more policy business and premium support through insurers.

The bill makes large feeding operations ineligible for conservation payments to build animal waste facilities and requires public reporting of livestock greenhouse gas emissions. It also directs conservation money toward pasture-based and antibiotic-reducing systems, shifting support toward their smaller competitors.

The bill creates tax credits for farmland transfers to beginning, veteran, and socially disadvantaged farmers, funds farm succession planning, gives priority access to local food programs, and adds assistance for organic transition under EQIP. These are the farmers the current subsidy and credit structure serves least.

industries.industry: Food-aid commodity shippers and agricultural exporters
industries.note: The bill removes the domestic procurement restriction in the Food for Peace Act, letting aid be provided as cash and locally purchased assistance rather than US-grown commodities shipped abroad. That historically redirects federal food-aid dollars away from US commodity and shipping interests and toward faster, cheaper assistance overseas.

industries.industry: Humane certification and organic food producers
industries.note: The bill creates an animal welfare certification tax credit and market-access programs for humanely raised livestock, and reserves at least 5 percent of EQIP funds for producers in independent humane certification programs. Producers already certified would gain a marketing advantage.
